rw: Net income is revenue minus cost of goods sold minus expenses. $450,000 less $270,000 less $120,000 leaves $60,000 of profit for the period.

ww.$330,000: $330,000 subtracts only the cost of goods sold from revenue and forgets the $120,000 of expenses. Net income takes away every cost, so it must be lower.
ww.$180,000: $180,000 is the gross profit, revenue minus cost of goods sold. Net income also subtracts the $120,000 of operating expenses that remain.
ww.$840,000: $840,000 adds all three figures together. Net income is found by subtracting the costs from revenue, so it can never be larger than revenue.

rw: A cash flow problem means cash runs short when bills fall due, even if the business is profitable on paper. Late customer payments or heavy spending can cause it.

ww.Having too many customers to serve them: Having too many customers is a good problem and does not cause a cash shortage. A cash flow problem is about money timing, not demand.
ww.Having too much profit, so the firm cann: Having too much profit is not a problem, and profit is not trapped cash. A cash flow problem is a shortage of cash, not a surplus of earnings.
ww.Having too many employees, so the firm c: Having many employees can raise costs, but the term cash flow problem is about whether cash on hand covers bills. Staff numbers are only one possible cause.

rw: Without training, a new hire does not know the procedures and makes errors. Poor onboarding and training is the likely cause, and good orientation prevents it.

ww.Too short a commute to work: A short commute does not cause mistakes on the job. It is a convenience for the employee and has nothing to do with skills or knowledge.
ww.Too many benefits to manage: Too many benefits to manage is an administrative issue for HR. It does not explain why a new hire without training makes many mistakes.
ww.Too much supervision for them: Too much supervision would help a new hire avoid errors, not cause them. The real gap is missing training, not too much guidance.

rw: A job description is a document listing the duties and requirements of a position. It guides recruiting, training and performance reviews.

ww.A list of company products and their pri: A job description lists the duties and requirements of a position, not products and prices. Price lists belong in a sales catalog.
ww.A record of past pay received by an empl: Past pay received is a payroll record kept for each employee. A job description describes a role, not what a person earned.
ww.A summary of interview questions the emp: Interview questions are prepared by the hiring team as a separate guide. A job description describes the role being filled, not the interview.

rw: Employee benefits are non-wage compensation such as health insurance, paid leave and retirement plans. They add value beyond the paycheck.

ww.The hourly wage that a worker is paid fo: An hourly wage is basic pay, which is direct compensation. Benefits are extras given on top of pay.
ww.A work assignment given to a worker by a: A work assignment is a task from a manager. It is part of the job, not a form of compensation.
ww.A fine for lateness that is taken out of: A fine for lateness is a penalty taken from pay. Benefits are positive extras such as insurance or paid leave.

rw: With the same salary, the offer that includes health insurance has higher total value. Benefits add to compensation beyond the paycheck.

ww.They are exactly equal in value: The two offers are not equal. Health insurance has real monetary value, since the employee would otherwise pay for it, so the offer that includes it is worth more.
ww.The one without insurance: The offer without insurance is worth less. With the same salary, the employee would still need to pay for coverage separately.
ww.Neither, benefits have no value: Benefits do have value. Health insurance can be worth thousands of dollars a year, so it makes one offer better than the other.

rw: Progressive discipline is a series of increasingly serious steps for repeated misconduct, such as a verbal warning, a written warning and then suspension or dismissal. It gives employees a chance to improve.

ww.Ignoring all misconduct and letting staf: Ignoring misconduct lets problems grow and is unfair to other workers. Progressive discipline responds to misconduct with steps.
ww.Firing at the first mistake, with no war: Firing at the first mistake with no warning is the opposite of progressive discipline. The approach is to escalate gradually.
ww.Rewarding misconduct with bonuses and ex: Rewarding misconduct would encourage more of it. Discipline is meant to correct behavior, not reward it.

rw: A customer ID number is unique to each customer. A unique identifier lets the table tell apart two customers who might share names or cities.

ww.Customer's city name: Many customers can live in the same city, so city name is not unique. It cannot identify one specific customer.
ww.Favorite color code: A favorite color code is shared by many people. It cannot tell one customer apart from another.
ww.Customer first name: Many customers share the same first name, such as Maria or John. A first name cannot serve as a unique identifier.

rw: Encryption scrambles data so that only authorized people with the key can read it. Even if stolen, the data is useless without that key.

ww.Making data easier to read by removing a: Encryption does not remove passwords to make data easier to read. It does the opposite, locking data so that only people with the key can read it.
ww.Copying data to another drive for backup: Copying data to another drive is a backup. Encryption scrambles data rather than copying it.
ww.Deleting data permanently so no one can: Deleting data so no one can read it is erasure. Encryption keeps the data but makes it unreadable to unauthorized people.

rw: Full-disk encryption scrambles everything on the laptop, so a thief cannot read the customer records without the key. It limits harm best.

ww.A longer warranty: A longer warranty covers repairs, not stolen data. It would not stop a thief from reading the records.
ww.A colorful laptop case: A colorful laptop case may make the laptop easier to spot, but it does not protect the data stored inside.
ww.Faster internet access: Faster internet does nothing to protect records on a stolen laptop. Protection needs security controls such as encryption.

rw: The four Ps of marketing are product, price, place and promotion. Together they are the decisions a business makes to reach its customers.

ww.People, profit, plans and paper: People, profit, plans and paper are not the marketing mix. They are not the four recognized Ps.
ww.Pay, purchase, produce and pack: Pay, purchase, produce and pack are business activities but not the marketing mix. The four Ps have specific names.
ww.Plan, perform, prove and publish: Plan, perform, prove and publish are not the marketing mix. The four Ps are product, price, place and promotion.

rw: Place covers where and how customers can buy a product. Adding delivery changes how the cakes reach buyers, so it changes the place element.

ww.Promotion: Promotion is how a business tells customers about a product, such as with ads. Adding delivery changes how customers get the cakes, not how they hear about them.
ww.Product: Product is what is sold, including features and quality. The cakes are unchanged, so the product element did not change.
ww.Price: Price is what customers pay. A delivery service changes how cakes reach customers, not what they cost.

rw: Positioning is how a brand wants customers to see it compared with rivals. It is the image the brand owns in customers' minds.

ww.Where a product is stored in a warehouse: Where a product is stored is a logistics matter. Positioning is about perception, not location in a warehouse.
ww.How a product is shipped to stores and t: How a product is shipped is distribution. Positioning is about how customers view the brand.
ww.Where a store is located in a town or a: The location of a store is a place decision. Positioning is the image of a brand, not a spot on a map.

rw: Just-in-time inventory means receiving goods only when they are needed. It lowers storage costs and waste, but needs dependable suppliers.

ww.Shipping goods once a year in one large: Shipping goods once a year in bulk is the opposite of just-in-time. JIT delivers small amounts often, exactly when needed.
ww.Ordering large amounts of goods in advan: Ordering large amounts in advance builds a big stock. Just-in-time does the reverse, keeping stock low.
ww.Holding large safety stocks always, at e: Holding large safety stocks at every site is costly. Just-in-time aims to cut inventory, not hold more.

rw: With so little buffer stock, a supplier delay can halt production. That fragility is the main risk of just-in-time.

ww.Too much unsold stock in storage: Too much unsold stock is the risk of overstocking. Just-in-time keeps stock low, so excess is not its risk.
ww.High storage costs for the stock: High storage costs come with large inventories. Just-in-time reduces them, so they are a benefit, not a risk.
ww.Wasted materials from overproduction: Wasted materials from overproduction come from making goods ahead of demand. Just-in-time makes goods only when needed.

rw: A purchase order is a document that requests goods or services from a supplier. It states the items, quantities, prices and delivery terms.

ww.A pay slip for an employee, listing wage: A pay slip shows wages paid. A purchase order is a request to a supplier.
ww.A bill sent to a customer after a sale h: A bill sent to a customer after a sale is an invoice. A purchase order is sent by the buyer, before delivery.
ww.A record of goods that arrived, signed b: A record of goods that arrived is a receiving report. A purchase order is made before the goods come.

rw: Capacity is the maximum amount a business can produce in a period. It limits how much the firm can sell without expanding.

ww.The minimum price of a product that a fi: The minimum price a firm will accept is a pricing floor. Capacity is about how much can be produced.
ww.The profit per unit that a firm earns on: Profit per unit is a measure of earnings. Capacity measures output.
ww.The number of customers served in a day: The number of customers served is a measure of demand. Capacity is about production.

rw: Lifelong learning means continuing to learn new skills throughout a career. It helps workers adapt as jobs and technology change.

ww.Avoiding new skills once a person has a: Avoiding new skills is the opposite of lifelong learning. It means learning continues throughout a career.
ww.Learning only from books in a library or: Learning only from books is too narrow. Lifelong learning includes training, experience and practice.
ww.Learning only in school and then stoppin: Learning only in school and then stopping is the opposite. Lifelong learning never stops.

rw: A SWOT analysis reviews strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats. It looks inside and outside the business to guide planning.

ww.A review of sales, wages, orders and tax: A review of sales, wages, orders and taxes describes financial reports. SWOT stands for something else.
ww.A review of suppliers, workers, owners a: Suppliers, workers, owners and traders are groups of people. They are not what SWOT stands for.
ww.A review of stocks, wealth, output and t: Stocks, wealth, output and trade of a nation are economic ideas. They are not the four parts of SWOT.

rw: A new competitor opening nearby is an external factor that could hurt the business. External negatives are called threats.

ww.Chance: A chance, or opportunity, is an external positive. A new competitor is a negative, so it is not a chance.
ww.Weakness: A weakness is an internal problem. A competitor is outside the business, so it is not a weakness.
ww.Strength: A strength is an internal advantage. A new competitor is external and harmful, so it is not a strength.

rw: A key performance indicator is a measurable value showing how well goals are being met. Examples are sales growth and customer satisfaction scores.

ww.A list of products that a firm sells to: A list of products a firm sells is a catalog. A KPI measures progress toward goals.
ww.A company's phone number and email addre: A phone number and email address are contact details. They are not a measure of performance.
ww.A customer's name and address kept on fi: A customer's name and address are records. They do not measure how well goals are being met.

rw: Increasing online sales by 15 percent in six months is specific, has a number and has a deadline. That makes it measurable.

ww.Try to improve things as much as we can: Trying to improve as much as we can has no number or deadline. Progress cannot be measured.
ww.Become popular soon with as many people: Becoming popular with as many people as possible is vague. There is no target to check.
ww.Do better next quarter than in the last: Doing better than last quarter has no size of improvement. It cannot show whether a goal was met.

rw: Operations management manages the activities that turn resources into goods or services. It focuses on efficiency, quality and cost.

ww.Setting the prices customers see in the: Setting prices is a marketing decision. Operations management runs the activities that make goods or services.
ww.Hiring new workers and handling their ye: Hiring and reviewing workers is human resources. Operations management focuses on production and service delivery.
ww.Choosing the advertisements that appear: Choosing ads is a marketing task. Operations deals with how products are made and delivered.

rw: Inventory management controls the amount of stock a business holds. It aims to avoid both running out and having too much.

ww.Deciding which employees work weekend sh: Scheduling shifts is workforce planning. Inventory management is about the stock a business holds.
ww.Counting the money in a cash register ea: Counting cash is a cash handling duty. Inventory management deals with goods, not money.
ww.Planning how a store will be decorated f: Planning holiday decorations is a visual merchandising task. It is not inventory management.

rw: Overordering ties money up in unsold coats. The store may have to cut prices later, which cuts profit.

ww.Higher profits because there is more to: More stock than can be sold does not raise profits. Unsold coats earn nothing and cost money to hold.
ww.Lower storage costs because stock is bul: Bulk buying does not lower storage costs when the goods stay unsold. Extra stock needs more space.
ww.Faster service for every customer who sh: Extra stock does not speed up service. It leaves goods unsold on the shelves.

rw: A stockout is running out of an item customers want to buy. It means lost sales and disappointed customers.

ww.Receiving an item late from a supplier e: A late delivery is a supply problem. A stockout is when an item is unavailable to customers.
ww.Selling an item at a deep discount on a: Deep discounting is a markdown. A stockout is a shortage, not a sale.
ww.Having far too much of an item in storag: Having far too much of an item is overstock, the opposite of a stockout.

rw: A reorder point is the stock level that triggers a new order. Ordering at that point keeps shelves filled until the delivery arrives.

ww.The price at which a product is sold: The selling price is a pricing decision. A reorder point is an inventory trigger.
ww.The number of items returned by customer: Returns are customer sends back. A reorder point concerns when to restock.
ww.The date a supplier is paid by the firm: The date a supplier is paid is a payment term. A reorder point is about stock levels.

rw: Reorder point equals daily use times lead time. 20 units a day over 5 days is 100 units, so reordering at 100 avoids a stockout.

ww.25 units: 25 units would run out in about a day and a bit. Delivery takes 5 days at 20 a day.
ww.500 units: 500 units far exceeds what is needed. The store only needs enough for the 5 days of delivery time.
ww.4 units: 4 units is far too few. The store sells 20 a day, so it would run out well before delivery.

rw: A vendor is a business that supplies goods or services to another business. Shops and factories depend on vendors for stock and materials.

ww.A customer who buys goods from a local b: A customer who buys goods is on the buying side. A vendor is on the supplying side.
ww.A rival firm that competes with the busi: A rival firm is a competitor. A vendor supplies to the business instead of competing with it.
ww.An employee who sells products in a shop: An employee who sells in a shop is a salesperson. A vendor is an outside supplier.

rw: Lead time is the time between placing an order and receiving it. Knowing it helps a business reorder before running out.

ww.The time between a sale and a refund bei: The time between a sale and a refund is a refund period. Lead time is about ordering.
ww.The time a product spends on a shelf bef: The time a product sits on a shelf is the holding period. Lead time is the wait for an order.
ww.The time a leader spends in meetings wit: A leader's time in meetings is not what lead time means. It is a supply term.

rw: Checking confirms quantity and condition match the order. It catches shortages and damage before paying.

ww.To raise the price of the goods that arr: Checking goods does not raise prices. It confirms what arrived.
ww.To make deliveries take longer to reach: Checking does not delay deliveries. It happens after goods arrive.
ww.To avoid recording it so the invoice sta: Not recording a shipment would leave records wrong. Goods should be checked and recorded.

rw: Efficiency is producing results with minimal waste of time and resources. It lowers costs and raises output.

ww.Working slowly to avoid mistakes of any: Working slowly to avoid mistakes is not efficiency. Efficiency also saves time.
ww.Spending more to produce less than befor: Spending more to produce less is the opposite of efficiency. Efficiency gets more from less.
ww.Producing as much waste as possible, sin: Producing waste is the opposite of efficiency. Efficient firms cut scrap.

rw: Productivity is the amount produced for the resources used. Higher productivity means more output from the same inputs.

ww.The number of stores that a firm owns no: The number of stores is a size measure. Productivity is output per input.
ww.The price of a finished product in the s: The price of a product is a pricing matter. Productivity measures output.
ww.The profit a firm makes during the year: Profit measures earnings. Productivity measures output for resources used.

rw: Productivity rose. The worker went from 40 items in 8 hours, or 5 an hour, to 60 in 8 hours, or 7.5 an hour.

ww.It cannot be measured, since days differ: Productivity can be measured. Output per hour is the usual measure, even when days differ.
ww.It decreased from 5 to 4 items per hour: Output rose from 40 to 60 items, so productivity increased. A decrease would need fewer items per hour.
ww.It stayed the same at 5 items per hour: The worker made more items in the same time, so productivity did not stay the same. It rose from 5 to 7.5 items an hour.

rw: A safety procedure reduces the chance of accidents and injuries. It sets clear steps for working safely.

ww.Increasing the speed of every task for w: Speeding up tasks is not the purpose of safety procedures. They can slow work slightly to keep people safe.
ww.Lowering the price of products sold in t: Prices are not set by safety procedures. They are rules for staying safe.
ww.Replacing the need for training of the n: Safety procedures do not replace training. Training helps staff follow them.

rw: Preventive maintenance is servicing equipment regularly to avoid breakdowns. It saves money and keeps work running.

ww.Replacing all equipment every month of t: Replacing all equipment every month is wasteful. Preventive maintenance services what the firm already has.
ww.Repairing equipment only after it fails: Repairing equipment only after it fails is reactive maintenance. Preventive maintenance acts before failure.
ww.Ignoring equipment problems until a mach: Ignoring problems until a machine stops is the opposite. Preventive maintenance fixes problems early.

rw: Servicing the oven every three months to avoid failure is preventive maintenance. It heads off problems before they happen.

ww.Price skimming plan: Price skimming is a pricing strategy. It has nothing to do with oven upkeep.
ww.Channel conflict risk: Channel conflict is a distribution issue. It does not describe servicing an oven.
ww.Emergency repair work: Emergency repair work happens after a failure. The regular servicing here is done to avoid one.

rw: Customer-focused operations run processes to meet customer needs for quality, speed and cost. The customer's needs shape how work is done.

ww.Ignoring what customer needs in order to: Ignoring customer needs to cut costs is not customer-focused. It puts cost ahead of customers.
ww.Setting rules that make buying harder, t: Rules that make buying harder push customers away. Customer-focused operations make buying easy.
ww.Making decisions without any feedback fr: Deciding without feedback ignores customers. A focus on customers listens to them.

rw: A soft skill is a personal ability such as communication or teamwork. Soft skills help people work well with others.

ww.Writing computer code, which is a techni: Writing computer code is a technical skill, not a soft skill. It is learned and measurable.
ww.Using accounting software, which is a te: Using accounting software is a technical skill. It is taught as a specific tool.
ww.Operating a machine, which is a technica: Operating a machine is a technical skill. Soft skills are about people.

rw: Preparing a spreadsheet budget is a technical skill. It uses software and math know-how that can be taught and measured.

ww.Listening well to your peers: Listening well to peers is a soft skill. It is an interpersonal ability.
ww.Showing empathy to coworkers: Showing empathy is a soft skill. It relates to people's feelings.
ww.Working in a team with coworkers: Working in a team is a soft skill. It is about cooperation, not a technical ability.

rw: A cover letter introduces you and explains why you fit a job. It highlights relevant skills and shows interest in the role.

ww.A list of every job you have held, with: A list of jobs with dates and pay is a resume or work history. A cover letter introduces you and explains why you fit the job.
ww.A request for a bank loan to start a new: A bank loan request is a financial document. A cover letter is part of a job application.
ww.A tax document that is filed with the go: A tax document is filed with the government. A cover letter goes to an employer.

rw: A reference is a person who can speak about your skills and character. Employers contact references to check what you have told them.

ww.A list of your hobbies and interests out: Hobbies and interests are details for a resume. A reference is a person, not a list.
ww.A copy of your diploma from the last sch: A diploma is proof of education. It is not a reference.
ww.A job offer letter that an employer has: A job offer is sent by an employer after hiring. It is not a reference.

rw: You ask first so they are prepared and willing to speak well of you. A surprised or unwilling reference can hurt your chances.

ww.Because the law requires it for every jo: No law requires asking, but it is polite and wise. The main reason is to make sure they are ready to speak for you.
ww.So they can pay your fees for school or: References do not pay your school fees. They speak about your abilities.
ww.So they can write your resume and know t: References do not write your resume. They give an opinion of your work.

rw: Time management means planning how to use time to meet goals. It involves priorities, schedules and deadlines.

ww.Working without breaks all day long: Working without breaks all day is not time management. It leads to tiredness and poor work.
ww.Doing tasks in random order each day: Doing tasks in random order is poor planning. Good time management uses priorities.
ww.Delaying all work until the deadline: Delaying work until the deadline is procrastination. It leaves no room for mistakes.

rw: An urgent and important task should be done first, since delay carries real consequences. The unimportant one can wait.

ww.Whichever is easier to do: Doing the easier task first is not the best choice. Priority should depend on importance and urgency.
ww.Neither, so as to avoid stress: Neither is a poor choice. Avoiding both leaves important work undone.
ww.The unimportant, non-urgent one: The unimportant, non-urgent task can wait. Doing it first wastes time needed for the urgent one.

rw: Workplace etiquette is accepted rules of polite and respectful behavior at work. It includes punctuality, courtesy and professionalism.

ww.A list of company products and prices gi: A list of products and prices is a catalog. Etiquette is about behavior.
ww.A set of tax rules that firms must follo: Tax rules are legal requirements. Etiquette is about manners at work.
ww.A dress code for parties and other fun s: A dress code for parties is not workplace etiquette. Etiquette applies to work behavior.

rw: Politely discussing the impact and agreeing on expectations addresses the problem respectfully. It gives the coworker a chance to change.

ww.Shout at the coworker in front of everyo: Shouting in front of everyone humiliates the coworker. It makes the problem worse.
ww.Gossip about the coworker to others in t: Gossip spreads rumors and breaks trust. It does not fix lateness.
ww.Ignore it forever and hope that it just: Ignoring it forever lets the problem continue. The team will keep losing time.

rw: An internship is short-term work experience that helps you learn on the job. It builds skills and contacts.

ww.A loan for students that is paid back af: A loan for students is a student loan. An internship is work experience.
ww.A permanent management role in a company: A permanent management role is a full job. An internship is short-term.
ww.A form for taxes that workers must file: A tax form is a government document. It is not an internship.

rw: Job shadowing means following a worker to learn what a job involves. It lets students see daily tasks without doing the job.

ww.Taking a worker's place permanently afte: Taking a worker's place permanently is a job change. Job shadowing is observing.
ww.Doing a worker's job for a month at full: Doing a worker's job for a month at full pay is a trial job. Shadowing is only watching.
ww.Working in a dark room for hours on end: Working in a dark room has no relation to the term. Shadowing means following someone.

rw: Professional organizations build skills, leadership and contacts. DECA and FBLA also offer competitions and networking.

ww.To guarantee a job after graduation: No organization can guarantee a job after graduation. DECA and FBLA build skills that help you compete.
ww.To skip school requirements and get a pa: Joining does not skip school requirements. Students must still meet them.
ww.To avoid any competition from other stud: These groups involve competition, not avoiding it. Competing builds skills.

rw: Networking is building relationships that can offer advice and opportunities. Contacts can lead to jobs, mentors and ideas.

ww.Selling to strangers on the street to ea: Selling to strangers is a sales activity. Networking builds mutual relationships.
ww.Working alone with no contact with any o: Working alone with no contact is the opposite. Networking depends on connecting with people.
ww.Connecting computers together over a wir: Connecting computers is a technical meaning. In careers it means connecting with people.

rw: Strategic planning means setting long-term goals and deciding how to reach them. It guides the whole organization over years.

ww.Ordering daily supplies for the kitchen: Ordering daily supplies is an operational task. Strategic planning looks far ahead.
ww.Scheduling this week's staff shifts and: Scheduling this week's shifts is short-term operational planning. Strategic planning is long-term.
ww.Filing patient charts and records in the: Filing charts is routine office work. It is not planning.

rw: Analyzing the market and its own strengths and weaknesses gives the facts needed to plan growth. It is the sensible first step.

ww.Hire many workers without a plan to brin: Hiring many workers without a plan may add cost with no sales. A plan should come first.
ww.Cut all advertising immediately and stop: Cutting advertising would likely reduce sales. It works against doubling revenue.
ww.Raise prices by half and hope that sales: Raising prices by half could drive customers away. It would not double sales.

rw: Benchmarking compares performance with the industry leader's. The delivery firm sees how far it is from the best.

ww.Market research: Market research studies customers. Comparing on-time rates with a leader is benchmarking.
ww.Stock counting: Stock counting checks inventory. It is not a comparison with a leader.
ww.Price fixing: Price fixing is an illegal agreement on prices. It is unrelated.

rw: Diversification means expanding into new products or markets. It spreads risk and creates new sources of income.

ww.Closing all branches of the business: Closing all branches is the opposite of expansion. Diversification adds new products or markets.
ww.Selling only one product for good: Selling only one product for good is the opposite. Diversification means offering more.
ww.Cutting all prices to the lowest level: Cutting prices to the lowest is a price strategy. It is not diversification.

rw: A shoe maker adding bags and belts enters new product lines. That is product diversification.

ww.Lower prices to gain share: Lowering prices to gain share is a pricing move. The shoe maker is adding products.
ww.Cost leadership strategy: Cost leadership is about the lowest costs. The shoe maker is expanding.
ww.Exit from the market: Exit from the market is leaving. The shoe maker is growing.

rw: A merger is two companies combining into one. It can create a larger firm with shared resources.

ww.One company splitting in two: One company splitting in two is a split or spin-off. A merger joins companies.
ww.A company closing a small branch: Closing a small branch is a downsizing. A merger is a combination.
ww.A company paying a big dividend: Paying a dividend shares profit with owners. It is not a merger.

rw: Customer segmentation groups customers by shared traits such as age or interests. It lets a business target each group.

ww.Treating every customer the same, whatev: Treating every customer the same is mass marketing. Segmentation tailors efforts.
ww.Counting customers only, with no traits: Counting customers with no traits is not segmentation. It requires grouping by traits.
ww.Ignoring customer data when planning any: Ignoring data is the opposite. Segmentation uses it.

rw: Student discounts for teens and wellness classes for adults over 50 target different segments with tailored offers. It fits the audience of each.

ww.Mass marketing to everyone with the same: Mass marketing sends one message to everyone. The gym tailors offers.
ww.Channel conflict between a firm and its: Channel conflict is a dispute between a firm and its sellers. It does not describe tailored offers.
ww.Price fixing between a few rival firms i: Price fixing is illegal collusion. It is unrelated.

rw: Promotion is communication that informs and persuades customers to buy. It includes ads, sales and publicity.

ww.Choosing where to sell a product, in a s: Choosing where to sell is place. Promotion communicates.
ww.Setting the price of a product for sale: Setting the price is price. Promotion informs and persuades.
ww.Designing the product so that it looks g: Designing the product is part of product development. Promotion is communication.

rw: Short videos on social media reach teens where they spend time. They suit the audience.

ww.Radio ads at 3 a.m. daily: Radio ads at 3 a.m. reach few teenagers. They are asleep.
ww.Printed notices in an office: Printed notices in an office reach working adults. They miss teenagers.
ww.Ads in a retirement newsletter: Ads in a retirement newsletter reach older readers. Teenagers do not read them.

rw: Customer loyalty is a customer's tendency to keep buying from the same business. Loyal customers also recommend it.

ww.A customer who avoids the store and neve: A customer who avoids the store is not loyal. Loyalty is returning.
ww.A customer who asks for refunds often an: Asking for refunds often and rarely buying again is not loyalty. It shows low engagement.
ww.A customer who buys only once and then n: Buying once and never returning is the opposite of loyalty. Loyal customers repeat.

rw: The marketing mix is the combination of product, price, place and promotion. A business adjusts these to reach customers.

ww.The mix of ingredients in a recipe used: A mix of recipe ingredients is cooking. The marketing mix is a business tool.
ww.The combination of tax and profit for th: Tax and profit are not the marketing mix. The mix is the four Ps.
ww.The combination of stores and offices of: Stores and offices are locations. They are not the marketing mix.

rw: Lowering the price changes the price element of the marketing mix. The company wants to attract buyers with a lower cost.

ww.Promotion: Promotion is how a business tells customers about a product. Lowering price does not change that.
ww.Place: Place is where products are sold. Lowering the price does not change location.
ww.Product: Product is the item itself. Lowering price does not change the product.

rw: A firewall is a security tool that controls traffic into and out of a network. It blocks unwanted connections.

ww.A program that edits photos and videos f: A program that edits photos is design software. A firewall protects networks.
ww.A wall that stops fires in buildings, ma: A wall that stops fires is a building feature. A firewall in computing is a security tool.
ww.A password for a website that a new user: A password is a login credential. A firewall filters network traffic.

rw: Multi-factor authentication requires two or more proofs of identity to sign in, such as a password and a code. It makes accounts much harder to break into.

ww.Writing a password on a note stuck to th: Writing a password on a note is a security risk. It is not authentication.
ww.Sharing a password with a team so all ca: Sharing a password weakens security. Multi-factor needs more proofs.
ww.Using one long password only, for every: One long password is only one factor. Multi-factor needs more.

rw: Unique strong passwords with multi-factor authentication give layered protection. An attacker needs more than a guessed password.

ww.Sharing passwords by email with all cowo: Sharing passwords by email exposes them. It weakens security.
ww.Reusing one password everywhere so there: Reusing one password everywhere is risky. If one account is hacked, the rest follow.
ww.Using easy-to-guess passwords that are s: Easy passwords are guessed quickly. They offer little protection.

ww.Encrypting data so that others cannot re: Encrypting data protects it. Data entry adds data.
ww.Printing data onto paper sheets for late: Printing data creates paper copies. Data entry adds data.

rw: Errors lead to wrong reports and decisions. Accurate entry keeps information reliable.

ww.Errors improve security for the whole sy: Errors do not improve security. They weaken data quality.

rw: An unexpected attachment may contain malware that harms your device. Opening it can infect systems.

ww.It makes email faster: Attachments do not make email faster. They make messages larger.
ww.It deletes spam for you: Attachments do not delete spam. They can carry it.

rw: Not opening it and reporting it is the safe choice. IT can check it and warn others.

ww.Open it to see what it is: Opening it to see what it is may infect the computer. Unknown attachments are a risk.

ww.Tracking employee shifts only and the ho: Tracking shifts only is too narrow. A database stores many kinds of records.
ww.Printing posters to advertise the firm's: Printing posters is a design job. A database holds data.

ww.Keeping files only on one computer in a: Keeping files on one computer is local storage. Cloud storage uses remote servers.
ww.Keeping files on paper in a cabinet in t: Paper files in a cabinet are physical storage. Cloud storage is digital.

rw: Secure cloud storage lets employees reach files from home safely. It keeps data protected.

ww.A single office computer: A single office computer cannot be reached from home. It does not meet the need.
ww.Paper files in a cabinet: Paper files cannot be accessed remotely. They must be in the office.
ww.USB drives passed around: USB drives passed around can be lost or infected. They are not secure or convenient.

rw: Customer-focused marketing plans around what customers need and value. It makes the product and message fit buyers.

ww.Planning marketing around rivals' logos: Planning around rivals' logos is competitor-focused. Customer-focused marketing looks at customers.
ww.Planning marketing around the lowest cos: Planning around the lowest cost is cost-focused. It does not put customers first.

rw: A production schedule is a plan showing what will be made, when and in what amount. It helps match output to demand.

ww.A list of customers who bought last year: A list of past customers is a sales record. It does not plan production.
ww.A chart of employee birthdays and work a: A chart of birthdays is an HR note. It is unrelated.

rw: A personal brand is the impression others have of your skills, reliability and character. It shapes opportunities at work.

ww.A tax form that employees must file with: A tax form is a government document. It has nothing to do with personal brand.
ww.A logo painted on your car, advertising: A logo painted on a car is advertising for a firm. A personal brand is a reputation.

rw: A contract needs an offer, acceptance and something of value exchanged by both sides. A lease with these elements is legally binding.

ww.A handshake and a friendly conversation: A handshake and a friendly chat do not make a written lease. The elements of a contract are needed.
ww.A verbal promise made in front of custom: A verbal promise before customers is not a lease agreement. It lacks the required elements.

rw: A trademark protects a name, logo or slogan that identifies a business's products. It stops others from copying the brand.

ww.To give the government control over the: A trademark does not give the government price control. It protects a brand identity.
ww.To guarantee that every product sold wil: A trademark cannot guarantee profit. It protects a name or logo.

rw: The store should get permission or a license from the copyright owner. Using the song without it would be infringement.

ww.A receipt showing the song was purchased: A receipt for a download does not give the right to use a song in an ad. Commercial use needs a license.
ww.Nothing, because songs on the radio are: Songs on the radio are not free to use in ads. Copyright still applies.
ww.A note from a customer saying they like: A customer's note has no legal effect. Only the owner can give permission.

rw: Negligence is a failure to use reasonable care. Leaving a wet floor with no warning is a failure that caused injury.

ww.Libel, a false statement that harms a na: Libel is a false written statement that harms a reputation. A wet floor injury is not defamation.
ww.Fraud, a deliberate deception to gain mo: Fraud is deliberate deception. The store did not deceive anyone.
ww.Bankruptcy, a process when debts go unpa: Bankruptcy is a process for unpaid debts. It does not apply to an injury claim.

rw: A warranty promises that the product will work or meet certain standards. If it fails, the buyer can seek repair or replacement.

ww.Lets the seller change the product after: A warranty does not let the seller change the product afterwards. It binds the seller.
ww.Requires the buyer to return the product: A warranty does not require return within one hour. It covers a longer period.
ww.Guarantees that the price of the product: A warranty does not guarantee a price. It covers quality.

rw: A corporation or LLC is a separate legal entity, so owners are not personally liable for business debts. Their risk is limited to what they invested.

ww.A general partnership of two close frien: A general partnership gives partners unlimited personal liability. It does not limit it.
ww.A sole proprietorship run by one person: A sole proprietorship has unlimited liability. The owner and business are the same legally.
ww.A business with no legal registration: A business with no registration offers no protection. Liability would be personal.

rw: Paying below minimum wage breaks wage laws, and a 14-hour shift on a school night for a 16-year-old breaks child labor rules. Both are likely violated.

ww.Zoning and building laws: Zoning and building laws concern property use. They are not about pay or hours.
ww.Antitrust and merger laws: Antitrust and merger laws concern competition. They are not about worker pay.
ww.Copyright and trademark laws: Copyright and trademark laws protect creative works. They do not apply here.

rw: An agent is a person authorized to act on behalf of another, the principal. The principal is bound by what the agent does within that authority.

ww.A person who buys goods only for his or: A person who buys only for personal use is a consumer. An agent acts for another.
ww.A person who lends money to businesses a: A person who lends money is a lender. An agent represents someone.
ww.A person who inspects a business for tax: A person who inspects for tax errors is an auditor. It is a different role.

rw: A written record shows the agreed terms and reduces disputes. It is easier to prove if there is a disagreement.

ww.Written contracts remove the need to fol: Written contracts do not remove the duty to follow the terms. They make the terms clear.
ww.Spoken agreements are always illegal in: Spoken agreements are not always illegal. They are harder to prove.
ww.Written contracts guarantee that no one: Written contracts cannot guarantee no disagreement. They reduce disputes.

rw: Failing to follow customs rules may cause delays, seizure or fines. Importers must comply.

ww.The shipment moves faster, skipping chec: Skipping checks is not allowed. Breaking rules brings problems.
ww.The company is exempt from future import: A company cannot become exempt by breaking customs rules. It would face trouble.

rw: Liability is a legal responsibility, often for debts or harm caused. A business can be liable to customers, lenders or others.

ww.The number of employees a company must h: The number of employees is a staffing decision. Liability is a legal duty.
ww.The value of a company's trademarks and: The value of trademarks is an asset. Liability is an obligation.
ww.The total revenue a business earns in a: Revenue is income. Liability is a responsibility.

rw: Shipping a week late after promising Friday delivery breaks the signed contract. That is a breach of contract.

ww.A patent infringement: A patent infringement is using an invention without permission. A late shipment breaks a delivery promise.
ww.A tariff on imports: A tariff is a tax on imports. It does not describe a late delivery.
ww.A merger of two firms: A merger combines firms. A late shipment is not a merger.

rw: The Federal Trade Commission enforces rules that protect consumers from deceptive advertising. It also guards fair competition.

ww.The Internal Revenue Service: The IRS collects taxes. It does not police advertising.
ww.The Federal Reserve Board: The Federal Reserve oversees the nation's money and banks. It does not enforce advertising rules.
ww.The SEC securities agency: The SEC oversees securities markets. It does not police ads for consumers.

rw: Environmental regulations limit pollution and protect natural resources. They aim to keep air, water and land healthy.

ww.To help businesses avoid paying all taxe: Environmental rules do not help avoid taxes. They are separate.
ww.To increase the prices of all products i: They do not exist to raise prices. Their goal is protection.
ww.To protect large companies from all comp: They do not protect big companies from competition. They apply to everyone.

rw: Antitrust law bans price fixing, where competitors secretly agree on prices. It protects consumers from artificially high prices.

ww.Child labor law limiting teen work: Child labor law limits teen work. It does not cover price agreements.
ww.Zoning law controlling land use: Zoning law controls how land is used. It does not apply.
ww.Copyright law protecting written works: Copyright law protects written works. It does not cover prices.

rw: A written memo or email with clear details is formal and keeps a record. It suits a detailed policy change.

ww.A rumor passed from coworker to coworker: A rumor is unreliable. It is not a formal channel.
ww.A quick hallway comment to a few workers: A quick hallway comment reaches only a few people. It lacks detail.
ww.A text message with no explanation given: A text with no explanation leaves people confused. It is not formal.

ww.It removes the need to ask any questions: Adapting does not remove questions. Questions help check understanding.

ww.Answer quickly without saying anything u: Answering without saying anything useful wastes the caller's time. A clear greeting helps.

ww.A pie chart: A pie chart shows parts of a whole. It does not show change over time well.
ww.A staff list: A staff list is a list of names. It shows no sales trend.
ww.A store photo: A store photo shows a place. It does not show data.

ww.To hide all the bad news from the reader: An executive summary does not hide bad news. It gives honest key points.
ww.To list every employee who worked on the: Listing everyone who worked on the project is credits. An executive summary gives key findings.
